newsitem.title: UK: Airlines seen on four-year profitability cycle.
newsitem.headline: Airlines seen on four-year profitability cycle.

text.p: The world's airlines will enjoy rising profits over the next three to four years and industry cyclicallity will diminish, NatWest Securities Ltd aviation analyst Mike Powell said.
He told IATA's 10th economic outlook conference on Tuesday this will be achieved against a background of improved airfares, reduced capacity, tighter finance and better cost management.
On the demand side, he predicted average traffic growth between 1995-99 of 5.9 percent which would outstrip capacity growth of 5.4 percent and give peak load factors of 68.4 percent in 1999.
The result would be a steady hike in industry net profits from US$5.5 billion in 1995 to a peak US$13.6 billion in 1999 with the prospects of "a better performance in the next downturn".

Citing the American Express European Airfares index, Powell said "in general price increases are sticking" and were up from two percent in second quarter 1992 to over five percent in the same period 1996.

This would be helped by significant capacity shortages this year and the next as the number of decommissioned aircraft continue to fall from 750 in 1995 and deliveries moved from 1996 trough of 420 new aircraft to 700 in 1999.

"But even in a tight capacity environment," he warned, "airlines must remain focused on costs." The industry had already been surprised at the resilience of oil prices which it had expected to soften as Iraq crude came onstream. But aviation fuel prices were up 35 percent against crude hikes of only 25 percent.

There was also too much cargo capacity following huge increases by KLM Royal Dutch Airlines NV and Deutsche Lufthansa AG. Restoration of service standards and step increases in the cost base were other factors bringing upward pressure.
Technology would no longer produce the 40-50 percent cost benefits of the past and airlines would look to consolidation and ways of using their networks more efficiently to contain costs.
"U.S. airlines are rebuilding their balance sheets and modernising their fleets, he added "but there will be no big orders. And Brussels is acting to restrict the abuses of state subsidies."
Elsewhere, shareholders and debt-holders were another constraining influence prioritising higher returns over big equipment orders.

Future industry winners would be those that stayed focused on costs; took early action against competitive threats; accepted a constant need to develop product; and built successful alliances, Powell said.

Losers would fail to cut costs or do so on a one-off basis; rest on flag carrier laurels; fail to innovate; and attempt to go it alone or neglect alliances. "No airlines can afford to be complacent," he concluded. -- Air Cargo Newsroom Tel+44 171 542 7706 Fax+44 171 542 5017
